title: He is with you wherever you are
word: He is with you wherever you are
hook: He is with you wherever you are (57:4)

segments.voice: Yesterday, the last of Al-Waqi'ah: none touch it but the purified, and your line was touched with purity. Did you wash before opening something that mattered? Today, Surah Al-Hadid, the Iron. Day six hundred twelve.

An airport gate at 5am. A hospital corridor. A new apartment with the boxes still taped shut. A hotel room in a city where you don't speak the language. Places like these can make a person feel strangely unhooked, as if they've left their whole life behind at the last address. Surah fifty-seven, Al-Hadid, has a short line for exactly that feeling. It sits in the middle of a verse about the heavens and the Throne, and it's only a few words long.

Surah Al-Hadid opens wide. Everything in the heavens and the earth glorifies God. Verse three gives four names in a row: he is the First and the Last, the Outward and the Inward. Then verse four. It describes God creating the heavens and the earth in six days, then establishing himself on the Throne. It says he knows what goes into the earth and what comes out of it, what comes down from the sky and what goes up into it. And then, in Pickthall: "and He is with you wheresoever ye may be." Wa huwa ma'akum ayna ma kuntum. Ma'akum: with you. Ayna ma kuntum: wherever you are. The verse ends: and God sees what you do. So how is God with you? Muslims have explained it in more than one way. Many classical commentators, like Ibn Kathir, said he is with you by his knowledge, his hearing and his sight, watching over you, while being above his Throne, as the same verse says. Others, especially in the Sufi tradition, dwell on the nearness itself, and read it with another verse: God is nearer to a person than their jugular vein. Both readings share one thing: there is no place where you are out of his sight. A famous hadith turns this into a way of worshipping. Asked what ihsan, excellence, is, the Prophet ﷺ said: to worship God as though you see him, and if you don't see him, he sees you. The airport gate, the hospital, the empty apartment: the verse doesn't make them less strange. It says you didn't arrive there alone.
screen: `THE FIRST, THE LAST, OUTWARD, INWARD.` · `WITH YOU, WHEREVER YOU ARE.` · `BY KNOWLEDGE AND SIGHT, OR NEARNESS.` · `IHSAN: AS THOUGH YOU SEE HIM.`

segments.voice: The practice: say it in the next new place. Before you get there, rehearse it now. Sit, and feel exactly where you are: the floor, the chair, the air on your skin. Breathe in: wherever. Breathe out: you are. Then picture the next unfamiliar place you'll walk into today or this week, a new room, a waiting area, a street. Imagine stepping in and saying the line quietly there. The bell holds the time.
He is with you wherever you are. Surah Al-Hadid, verse four: wa huwa ma'akum ayna ma kuntum. Today's word.

segments.voice: Your line: wherever you are. Today, the next time you walk into a place you haven't been, say it under your breath at the door. Day six hundred twelve.

howItsDone: Muslims often recall this verse when traveling or in unfamiliar places; the idea of ihsan, worshipping as though one sees God, is taught from the hadith of Jibril as the highest level of faith.

original.say: wa HU-wa ma-'A-kum AY-na maa KUN-tum
original.note: Arabic: and He is with you wherever you are. ma'a means with; ayna ma, wherever.

trapdoor: what you thought: a comforting line about God being everywhere.
what it means: in a verse about the Throne, God says he is with you wherever you are, and sees what you do.
what a scholar hears: ma'iyya, divine 'withness', read by Ibn Kathir and others as knowledge and oversight, by Sufi readers as nearness, alongside 50:16; ihsan from the hadith of Jibril (Muslim 8).
